did_you_know.text: Did you know? The chapter opens with a question about a figure coming from Edom, from Bozrah, dressed in splendor and garments stained with blood. The figure declares that he speaks righteously and is mighty to save.
Did you know? The figure describes his action as the treading of a winepress: he says that he trod the winepress alone, and that no one from the nations was with him.
Did you know? Two central concepts appear together in the chapter: “the day of vengeance” and “the year of my redeemed”—the day of vengeance and the time of redemption.
Did you know? The figure emphasizes that he found no helper or supporter, so his own arm and his wrath accomplished the victory.
Did you know? After describing vengeance, the chapter turns to recounting the Lord’s acts of kindness and praises, especially his goodness and compassion toward the house of Israel.
Did you know? The Lord is described as saying of Israel, “They are indeed my people,” and as viewing them as children who would not be false. As a result, he became their Savior.
Did you know? The chapter describes Israel’s redemption in terms of love, compassion, and carrying: the Lord redeemed them, took them up, and carried them throughout all the days of old.
Did you know? Alongside its description of the Lord’s kindness, the chapter says that Israel rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit. As a result, the Lord became their enemy and fought against them.
Did you know? In its description of how the people were led in the past, the chapter mentions Moses, the exodus from Egypt, the parting of the waters, and the Holy Spirit given among the people.
Did you know? In its final section, the chapter becomes a plea: Israel asks the Lord to look down from heaven, stir up his zeal and compassion, and remember that he is their Father and Redeemer.
